questions.question: How do class, sexuality, and literary culture intersect to enable or hinder Orlando’s pursuit of fulfilment? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• In Virginia Woolf's novel, Orlando's aristocratic position provides access to literary circles,
  • education, and freedom from economic necessity. At the same time, Orlando's homoerotic
  • desires and eventual gender transformation represent desires impossible within
  • heteronormative bourgeois marriage structures [CO2].
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss the function of “Love Laws” in the novel as informal mechanisms regulating romantic and sexual relationships to reinforce social hierarchies. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• In Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things (1997), the concept of "Love Laws" functions as
  • the central mechanism through which caste, class, and gender hierarchies are maintained and
  • policed in postcolonial Kerala. The laws decree that cross-caste romantic or sexual
  • relationships constitute the most severe transgression of social order [CO3].
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Traditional views of sexual repression. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Victorian and patriarchal frameworks conceptualised female sexuality as something requiring
  • suppression for maintaining social order, morality, and masculine authority.
  • Female sexuality as dangerous - Public/private dichotomy - Medicalisation (women's
  • sexuality was pathologised) - Compliance through shame [CO1].
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: How does Woolf’s vision of identity anticipate current debates about intersectionality and inclusivity? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Virginia Woolf's conceptualisation of identity prefigures contemporary intersectional
  • approaches by resisting singular, unified identity categories.
  • Fluidity and multiplicity - Rejection of essential categories - Material conditions and
  • consciousness [CO2].
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Analyse Nyasha’s rebellion in the context of cultural conflict and psychological distress. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Nyasha exists within irreconcilable cultural demands - the colonial mission school education
  • valorises "European" femininity, individualism, and intellectual development, while Shona
  • family structures emphasise female submission, duty, and communal belonging. The
  • psychological distress emerges from being educated beyond "appropriate" femininity while
  • remaining subject to patriarchal control [CO3].
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Define “gender identity” and explain its importance in understanding gender diversity. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Gender identity refers to an individual's internal, deeply felt sense of their own gender, which
  • may or may not correspond to the sex assigned at birth. It encompasses how one understands,
  • experiences, and expresses oneself as masculine, feminine, non-binary, or otherwise
  • gendered. Recognition of lived experience - Moving beyond essentialism- Inclusion and
  • equity - Understanding oppression- Intersectionality [CO1].
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Analyse the symbolic significance of public spectacle in Red, White & Royal Blue in shaping audience perceptions of queer romance and the concept of visibility in contemporary society. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:

questions.question: Analyse the tension between tradition and modernity as experienced by female characters in Nervous Conditions. / [CO3] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• The tension between tradition and modernity forms the core structural conflict in Nervous
  • Conditions, experienced acutely by female characters caught between Shona customary
  • practices and colonial "civilisation." Tambu’s pursuit of modernity through the mission
  • school produces psychological conflict and self-estrangement. Unable to synthesise these
  • contradictions, Nysha experiences psychological fragmentation and self-harm. Maiguru
  • represents an older generation attempting adaptation rather than resolution [CO3].

questions.question: Describe the events in The Sun Also Rises. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Ernest Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises (1926), also published as Fiesta, follows Jake
  • Barnes and his circle of expatriate friends in post-World War I Europe. The novel traces
  • Jake's relationship with Lady Brett Ashley, an aristocratic English woman separated from her
  • husband, who circulates through the expatriate community in Paris. Jake loves Brett, but their
  • relationship remains unconsummated - Jake's war wound has left him sexually impotent,
  • creating the novel's central tragedy. The opening establishes the aimless hedonism of 1920s
  • expatriate lifein Paris. Jake and his friends (Robert Cohn, Bill Gorton, and others) drift
  • through bars, cafés, and social gatherings. Brett arrives, and her charismatic presence
  • magnetises the group. The central action involves the group's trip to Pamplona for the San
  • Fermín festival and bullfighting. This pilgrimage represents both retreat from modern urban
  • life and confrontation with authentic passion and danger through bullfighting's spectacle.
  • During the festival, complex romantic dynamics emerge. Robert Cohn, an American writer,
  • attempts to claim Brett as his lover, but she leaves him for Pedro Romero, a young, beautiful
  • bullfighter. Jake experiences acute jealousy and pain. Bill Gorton offers comic relief and
  • commentary on the destructive romance [CO3].
